claim: Context promotes the visual recognition of objects.
source: Despite evidence that context promotes the visual recognition of objects, decades of research have led to the pervasive notion that the object processing pathway in primate cortex consists of multiple areas that each process the intrinsic features of a few particular categories (e.g. faces, bodies, hands, objects, and scenes).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on context and object recognition.

claim: The object processing pathway in primate cortex consists of multiple areas that each process the intrinsic features of a few particular categories (e.g. faces, bodies, hands, objects, and scenes).
source: Despite evidence that context promotes the visual recognition of objects, decades of research have led to the pervasive notion that the object processing pathway in primate cortex consists of multiple areas that each process the intrinsic features of a few particular categories (e.g. faces, bodies, hands, objects, and scenes).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to decades of research establishing this notion.

claim: Category-selective neurons do not code individual categories in isolation but are also sensitive to object relationships that reflect statistical regularities of the experienced environment.
source: Here we report that such category-selective neurons do not in fact code individual categories in isolation but are also sensitive to object relationships that reflect statistical regularities of the experienced environment.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Face-selective neurons respond not just to an image of a face, but also to parts of an image where contextual cues—for example a body—indicate a face ought to be, even if what is there is not a face.
source: We show by direct neuronal recording that face-selective neurons respond not just to an image of a face, but also to parts of an image where contextual cues—for example a body—indicate a face ought to be, even if what is there is not a face.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct neuronal recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Faces are usually conjoined to a body, and this regular structure influences how we perceive and interact with faces.
source: We do not often see faces in isolation, rather our experience of faces is embedded within a contextually rich environment – a face is usually conjoined to a body – and this regular structure influences how we perceive and interact with faces (Bar and Ullman, 1996; Meeren et al., 2005; Rice et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Bar and Ullman, 1996; Meeren et al., 2005; Rice et al., 2013).

claim: Neurons critical for the perception of faces do not respond to bodies, and vice versa.
source: However, it is generally found that neurons critical for the perception of faces (Afraz et al., 2015; Afraz et al., 2006; Moeller et al., 2017) do not respond to bodies, and vice versa (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Freiwald et al., 2009; Kiani et al., 2007; Tsao et al., 2006), suggesting that such neurons code for the intrinsic features of either faces or bodies but not both (Chang and Tsao, 2017; Issa and DiCarlo, 2012; Leopold et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior neuronal recording studies (Afraz et al., 2015; Afraz et al., 2006; Moeller et al., 2017; Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Freiwald et al., 2009; Kiani et al., 2007; Tsao et al., 2006).

claim: Face and body neurons code for the intrinsic features of either faces or bodies but not both.
source: However, it is generally found that neurons critical for the perception of faces (Afraz et al., 2015; Afraz et al., 2006; Moeller et al., 2017) do not respond to bodies, and vice versa (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Freiwald et al., 2009; Kiani et al., 2007; Tsao et al., 2006), suggesting that such neurons code for the intrinsic features of either faces or bodies but not both (Chang and Tsao, 2017; Issa and DiCarlo, 2012; Leopold et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Chang and Tsao, 2017; Issa and DiCarlo, 2012; Leopold et al., 2006) and is inferred from the observation that face neurons don't respond to bodies and vice versa.

claim: Studies typically probe neural function by presenting objects in isolation, independent of their typical context.
source: These studies typically probe neural function by presenting objects in isolation, independent of their typical context.
evidence: This is a characterization of prior experimental methodology, supported by knowledge of the field.

claim: Recordings were made from two face-selective domains within inferotemporal cortex (IT) in two macaque monkeys while they viewed complex natural images.
source: We recorded from two face-selective domains within inferotemporal cortex (IT) in two macaque monkeys while they viewed complex natural images.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Face cells demonstrate a large contextual surround tuned to entities that normally co-occur with faces.
source: Thus, we find that face cells demonstrate a large contextual surround tuned to entities that normally co-occur with faces.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: IT neurons do not represent objects in isolation, but are also sensitive to object relationships that reflect statistical regularities of the experienced environment.
source: These results reveal surprisingly complex and heterogeneous inputs to face-selective neurons, suggesting that IT neurons do not represent objects in isolation, but are also sensitive to object relationships that reflect statistical regularities of the experienced environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Recordings were made simultaneously from face-selective neurons in the fMRI-defined middle lateral (ML) and posterior lateral (PL) face patches in one rhesus macaque monkey, Monkey 1, and from ML in another monkey, Monkey 2, using chronically implanted 32-channel multi-electrode arrays.
source: We recorded simultaneously from face-selective neurons in the fMRI-defined middle lateral (ML) and posterior lateral (PL) face patches in one rhesus macaque monkey, Monkey 1, and from ML in another monkey, Monkey 2, using chronically implanted 32-channel multi-electrode arrays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When mapped using ~2°x2° faces and round non-face objects, the activating regions were small (1-3°), located in the central visual field (within 2° of fixation, and largely contralateral).
source: When mapped using ~2°x2° faces and round non-face objects, the activating regions were small (1-3°), located in the central visual field (within 2° of fixation, and largely contralateral; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the receptive field properties of the recorded neurons, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All the visually responsive sites in both monkeys responded more to faces than to any other category when tested with images of faces, hands, bodies, and objects presented centered on the activating region.
source: When tested with images of faces, hands, bodies (only for ML arrays), and objects presented centered on this activating region, all the visually responsive sites in both monkeys responded more to faces than to any other category (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the category selectivity of the recorded neurons, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: In both monkeys' ML face patches, responses to faces were much larger than to non-face images (mean channel face vs. non-face selectivity indices = 0.63 +/- 0.06 STD and 0.64 +/- 0.14 for Monkey's 1 and 2).
source: In particular, in both monkeys' ML face patches, responses to faces were much larger than to non-face images (mean channel face vs. non-face selectivity indices = 0.63 +/- 0.06 STD and 0.64 +/- 0. 14 for Monkey's 1 and 2)
evidence: This quantifies the face selectivity of ML neurons.

claim: In both monkeys' ML face patches, responses to faces were much larger than to bodies (mean channel face vs. body selectivity indices = 0.77 +/- 0.11 and 0.60 +/- 0.21).
source: In particular, in both monkeys' ML face patches, responses to faces were much larger than to non-face images (mean channel face vs. non-face selectivity indices = 0.63 +/- 0.06 STD and 0.64 +/- 0. 14 for Monkey's 1 and 2) or to bodies (mean channel face vs. body selectivity indices = 0.77 +/- 0.11 and 0.60 +/- 0.21).
evidence: This quantifies the face vs. body selectivity of ML neurons.

claim: Responses to bodies were weak in ML (body vs. object selectivity indices = −0.54 +/- 0.17 STD and 0.04 +/- 0.27 for ML in both Monkeys 1 and 2).
source: Responses to bodies were weak (body vs. object selectivity indices = −0.54 +/- 0.17 STD and 0.04 +/- 0.27 for ML in both Monkeys 1 and 2).
evidence: This quantifies the body selectivity of ML neurons.

claim: A strong preference for faces over other categories is consistent with many previous studies.
source: Such a strong preference for faces over other categories is consistent with many previous studies (Bell et al., 2011; Tsao et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Bell et al., 2011; Tsao et al., 2006).

claim: The array in Monkey 1's PL face patch was less face selective (mean channel face vs. non-face selectivity indices = 0.24 +/- 0.07 STD).
source: The array in Monkey 1's PL face patch was less face selective (mean channel face vs. non-face selectivity indices = 0.24 +/- 0.07 STD)
evidence: This quantifies the face selectivity of PL neurons.

claim: Responses to hands were weak in PL (mean channel hands vs. objects indices = 0.04 +/- 0.02 STD).
source: and responses to hands were weak (mean channel hands vs. objects indices = 0.04 +/- 0.02 STD), also consistent with previous work (Issa and DiCarlo, 2012).
evidence: This quantifies the hand selectivity of PL neurons and is consistent with prior work (Issa and DiCarlo, 2012).

claim: The recording site illustrated in Figure 1C responded most strongly to the parts of that image that contained monkey faces.
source: The recording site illustrated in Figure 1C responded most strongly to the parts of that image that contained monkey faces.
evidence: This describes the response properties of a specific recording site, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: Within each array the responses were all face selective and showed similar receptive-field locations and spatial response patterns to complex scenes.
source: Within each array the responses were all face selective (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and showed similar receptive-field locations and spatial response patterns to complex scenes (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 4).
evidence: This describes the uniformity of responses across channels within each array, supported by Figure 1—figure supplements 2, 3, and 4.

claim: All three arrays showed responsiveness that was spatially specific to the faces in each image.
source: Consistent with the PSTHs of image categories presented in isolation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), all three arrays showed responsiveness that was spatially specific to the faces in each image.
evidence: This describes the spatial specificity of responses, supported by Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: ML recording sites were more face selective and had longer latencies compared to the PL sites during simultaneous recordings.
source: Consistent with prior physiological and anatomical work suggesting that face patches are organized into a hierarchy that varies along the posterior-anterior axis (Grimaldi et al., 2016; Moeller et al., 2008), ML recording sites were more face selective and had longer latencies compared to the PL sites during simultaneous recordings (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This describes the hierarchical organization of face patches, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and citations to prior work (Grimaldi et al., 2016; Moeller et al., 2008).

claim: Activity specific to the eyes is apparent in both PL and ML.
source: Activity specific to the eyes is apparent in both PL and ML (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of face-selective activity, supported by Figure 2.

claim: Activity encompassing the rest of the face emerges at longer latencies.
source: Activity encompassing the rest of the face emerges at longer latencies.
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of face-selective activity.

claim: Prior work shows a preference for the contralateral eye in area PL that emerges between 60–80 ms post stimulus onset and longer latencies for images without a contralateral eye.
source: This is consistent with prior work showing a preference for the contralateral eye in area PL that emerges between 60–80 ms post stimulus onset and longer latencies for images without a contralateral eye (Issa and DiCarlo, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Issa and DiCarlo, 2012).

claim: A similar shift in response latencies was evident when replacing the eyes with a visible occluder, the background of the image, and surrounding texture of the face.
source: A similar shift in response latencies was evident when replacing the eyes with a visible occluder, the background of the image, and surrounding texture of the face (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the effect of eye occlusion on response latencies, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both PL and ML exhibited a shift in the latency for activity corresponding to faces without eyes, but PL activity still preceded ML.
source: In our recordings, both PL and ML exhibited a shift in the latency for activity corresponding to faces without eyes, but PL activity still preceded ML (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This describes the hierarchical processing of faces with and without eyes, supported by Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of eyes, face-specific activity still emerges across the ventral visual hierarchy in a bottom-up fashion.
source: indicating that in the absence of eyes, face-specific activity still emerges across the ventral visual hierarchy in a bottom-up fashion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PL activity precedes ML activity even for eyeless faces.

claim: When presented with images in which the face was occluded by some object in the image, the face cells in ML in both monkeys responded to the part of the image where the face ought to be, more than to non-face parts of the images.
source: When presented with images in which the face was occluded by some object in the image, surprisingly, the face cells in ML in both monkeys responded to the part of the image where the face ought to be, more than to non-face parts of the images (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a key finding of the study, supported by Figure 3.

claim: Responses to occluded faces were apparent in individual channels.
source: Though noisier than the population average, responses to occluded faces were apparent in individual channels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the robustness of the occluded face response, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The population-level activity to occluded faces was reliably higher than the average response to the rest of each image (t-test across 12 and 10 images for Monkeys 1 and 2, respectively; p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: Across all stimuli, the population-level activity to occluded faces was reliably higher than the average response to the rest of each image (t-test across 12 and 10 images for Monkeys 1 and 2, respectively; p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This quantifies the statistical significance of the occluded face response.

claim: The responses to occluded faces on average were slower than the responses to intact faces by ~30–40 ms.
source: Interestingly, the responses to occluded faces on average were slower than the responses to intact faces by ~30–40 ms (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of occluded face responses, supported by Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The latency of responses to occluded faces was similar to that to eyeless faces.
source: The latency of responses to occluded faces was similar to that to eyeless faces (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This compares the latencies of responses to occluded and eyeless faces, supported by Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: By 119 ms and 139 ms post stimulus onset for Monkey 1 and Monkey 2, respectively, the responses to occluded faces were significantly larger than the responses to the rest of the image.
source: By 119 ms and 139 ms post stimulus onset for Monkey 1 and Monkey 2, respectively, the responses to occluded faces were significantly larger than the responses to the rest of the image.
evidence: This quantifies the timing of the occluded face response.

claim: Responses to non-occluded versions of these faces were significantly larger than the responses to the rest of the image starting at 92 ms and 97 ms post stimulus onset for Monkey 1 and Monkey 2, respectively.
source: In contrast, responses to non-occluded versions of these faces were significantly larger than the responses to the rest of the image starting at 92 ms and 97 ms post stimulus onset for Monkey 1 and Monkey 2, respectively.
evidence: This quantifies the timing of the intact face response.

claim: When presented with people wearing masks, baskets or paper bags covering their faces, cells in ML responded to the masked faces.
source: Furthermore, when presented with people wearing masks, baskets or paper bags covering their faces, cells in ML responded to the masked faces (Figure 4).
evidence: This is another key finding of the study, supported by Figure 4.

claim: Responses to masked faces were also apparent in individual channels.
source: Similar to the occluded faces, responses to masked faces were also apparent in individual channels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the robustness of the masked face response, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The population-level responses to masked faces were consistently stronger than average responses to the rest of each image (t-test across 10 and 11 images for Monkeys 1 and 2, respectively; p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: The population-level responses to masked faces varied in magnitude and timing but were consistently stronger than average responses to the rest of each image (t-test across 10 and 11 images for Monkeys 1 and 2, respectively; p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This quantifies the statistical significance of the masked face response.

claim: The latency of responses to masked faces was similar to that to eyeless faces.
source: The latency of responses to masked faces (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3) was also similar to that to eyeless faces (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This compares the latencies of responses to masked and eyeless faces, supported by Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Face cells in PL also responded more to occluded faces than to the non-face parts of the images (p<0.05, FDR corrected).
source: Face cells in PL also responded more to occluded faces than to the non-face parts of the images (Figure 4—figure supplement 4; p<0.05, FDR corrected).
evidence: This describes the occluded face response in PL, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cells in PL also responded on average more strongly to masked faces than to other parts of each image, but this difference was not significant (p>0.05, FDR corrected).
source: Though cells in PL also responded on average more strongly to masked faces than to other parts of each image, this difference was not significant (Figure 4—figure supplement 4; p>0.05, FDR corrected).
evidence: This describes the masked face response in PL, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Responses to occluded faces were more prominent at later stages of the ventral visual hierarchy.
source: Thus, responses to occluded faces were more prominent at later stages of the ventral visual hierarchy.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of PL and ML responses to occluded and masked faces.

claim: In both monkeys' ML patches, responses to the non-face object positioned above a body were larger than responses to the same object when not above a body, both at the population level and in individual channels.
source: In both monkeys' ML patches, responses to the non-face object positioned above a body were larger than responses to the same object when not above a body, both at the population level (Figure 5) and in individual channels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a key finding demonstrating the body facilitation effect, supported by Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Population-level responses to face-swapped images varied in magnitude and latency, but responses to non-face objects were consistently stronger when positioned above a body than when positioned elsewhere (t-test across 8 and 15 images for M1 and M2, respectively; p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: Similar to the occluded and masked faces, population-level responses to these face-swapped images varied in magnitude and latency, but responses to non-face objects were consistently stronger when positioned above a body than when positioned elsewhere (t-test across 8 and 15 images for M1 and M2, respectively; p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This quantifies the statistical significance of the body facilitation effect.

claim: The latency of responses to the non-face object above a body was comparable to that to eyeless faces.
source: Similar to the occluded and masked faces, the latency of responses to the non-face object above a body (Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3) was comparable to that to eyeless faces (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This compares the latencies of responses to non-face objects above bodies and eyeless faces, supported by Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Cells in PL also responded on average more strongly to objects on top of bodies, but this difference was not significant (p>0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: Though cells in PL also responded on average more strongly to objects on top of bodies, this difference was not significant (Figure 4—figure supplement 4; p>0.05, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This describes the body facilitation effect in PL, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Responses in ML to a non-face image were facilitated by a body below it.
source: Thus, responses in ML to a non-face image were facilitated by a body below it.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the face-swapped image experiment.

claim: Responses to faces above bodies were indistinguishable from responses to disembodied faces.
source: Instead, responses to faces above bodies were indistinguishable from responses to disembodied faces (Figure 6, leftmost; Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2, top two rows).
evidence: This describes the lack of body facilitation for intact faces, supported by Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Responses to face-shaped noise patches, face outlines, and non-face objects were facilitated by the presence of a body positioned below.
source: In contrast, responses to face-shaped noise patches (i.e. where face pixels were replaced by random 3-color channel pixel values), face outlines, and non-face objects were facilitated by the presence of a body positioned below (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This describes the body facilitation effect for face-ambiguous stimuli, supported by Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Face-shaped noise patches and face-shaped outlines both elicited responses above baseline even in the absence of the body.
source: Face-shaped noise patches and face-shaped outlines both elicited responses above baseline even in the absence of the body (middle two columns).
evidence: This describes the baseline response to face-shaped stimuli.

claim: The responses to face-shaped noise and outlines when placed above a body were significantly larger (p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: Importantly, the responses to these images when placed above a body were significantly larger (p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This quantifies the statistical significance of the body facilitation effect for face-shaped stimuli.

claim: Non-face objects activated these neurons only when placed above bodies (p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: Further, non-face objects activated these neurons only when placed above bodies (Figure 6 rightmost column, p<0.05, FDR-corrected; Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2, bottom row).
evidence: This describes the body facilitation effect for non-face objects, supported by Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Bodies facilitate responses of face cells only when the presence of a face is ambiguous.
source: Together, these data suggest a ceiling effect--that bodies facilitate responses of face cells only when the presence of a face is ambiguous.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that bodies facilitate responses to face-ambiguous stimuli but not intact faces.

claim: These neurons respond to the region above a body even if no foreground object is present.
source: Further, these neurons respond to the region above a body even if no foreground object is present (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the response to headless bodies, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the absence of a face, the presence of a body below the receptive field appears to be sufficient for driving these face-selective cells.
source: In the absence of a face, the presence of a body below the receptive field appears to be sufficient for driving these face-selective cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments with face-ambiguous stimuli and headless bodies.

claim: Headless bodies produced activation maps that were similarly maximal at positions in which a face ought to be centered on the cells' activating region, not just when the body was positioned below the activating region.
source: Headless bodies produced activation maps that were similarly maximal at positions in which a face ought to be centered on the cells' activating region, not just when the body was positioned below the activating region (Figure 7A, bottom two rows).
evidence: This describes the spatial specificity of the body facilitation effect, supported by Figure 7A.

claim: Preferred body orientation systematically varied such that the preferred body orientation at that spatial location positioned the face, or where the face ought to be, within the RF center.
source: In experiments both with and without heads, preferred orientation systematically varied such that the preferred body orientation at that spatial location positioned the face, or where the face ought to be, within the RF center.
evidence: This describes the relationship between body orientation and face position, inferred from the composite orientation maps.

claim: These neurons were also responsive when the feet landed in the activating region, for the bodies without heads, and, to a lesser extent, the bodies with heads.
source: Interestingly, these neurons were also responsive when the feet landed in the activating region, for the bodies without heads, and, to a lesser extent, the bodies with heads.
evidence: This describes an additional aspect of the body facilitation effect.

claim: Both end-of-a-body and above-a-body are cues that a face might be expected.
source: This was especially apparent for inverted bodies, suggesting that both end-of-a-body and above-a-body are cues that a face might be expected.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that neurons respond to both ends of inverted bodies.

claim: Face cells are maximally responsive to where a face would be expected, largely irrespective of the body orientation.
source: The surprising result that face cells are maximally responsive to where a face would be expected, largely irrespective of the body orientation, indicates that the responses to occluded faces documented in Figures 3 and 4 are not responses merely to bodies located below the cells' face-selective regions, but instead reflect information about where a face ought to be, for a given body configuration.
evidence: This is a key conclusion drawn from the body orientation experiment.

claim: For whole body images, there was only a brief difference in activity between upright and inverted configurations during the initial response.
source: For whole body images, there was only a brief difference in activity between upright and inverted configurations during the initial response.
evidence: This describes the inversion effect for intact faces with bodies.

claim: For face-shaped noise, the response was substantially larger for the upright (vs. inverted) configurations for the duration of the response.
source: For face-shaped noise, the response was substantially larger for the upright (vs. inverted) configurations for the duration of the response.
evidence: This describes the inversion effect for face-shaped noise with bodies.

claim: Differences in response magnitudes within IT face domains for upright vs. inverted faces are modest or not consistently found in humans or monkeys.
source: While reaction time differences between upright and inverted faces are robust and reliable across studies (Leehey et al., 1978; Yin, 1969), differences in response magnitudes within IT face domains are modest or not consistently found in humans (Aguirre et al., 1999; Haxby et al., 1999; Kanwisher et al., 1998) or monkeys (Bruce, 1982; Pinsk et al., 2009; Rosenfeld and Van Hoesen, 1979; Taubert et al., 2015; Tsao et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Leehey et al., 1978; Yin, 1969; Aguirre et al., 1999; Haxby et al., 1999; Kanwisher et al., 1998; Bruce, 1982; Pinsk et al., 2009; Rosenfeld and Van Hoesen, 1979; Taubert et al., 2015; Tsao et al., 2006).

claim: The lack of a strong inversion effect for intact-faces-over-bodies compared to a stronger inversion effect for non-face-objects-above-bodies could reflect a ceiling effect, or it could mean that, in the presence of a face, tuning is more flexible and more invariant to spatial transformations.
source: The lack of a strong inversion effect for intact-faces-over-bodies compared to a stronger inversion effect for non-face-objects-above-bodies could reflect a ceiling effect, or it could mean that, in the presence of a face, tuning is more flexible and more invariant to spatial transformations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the inversion effect results.

claim: There was a large, sustained difference in response magnitude between upright and inverted face-shaped noise patches with bodies.
source: In contrast to responses to intact faces, there was a large, sustained difference in response magnitude between upright and inverted face-shaped noise patches with bodies (Figure 7B; noise atop bodies)
evidence: This describes the inversion effect for face-shaped noise with bodies, supported by Figure 7B.

claim: The body facilitation is maximal when the presence of a face is ambiguous and above a body.
source: suggesting that the body facilitation is maximal when the presence of a face is ambiguous and above a body.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the inversion effect results.

claim: The preference for upright vs. inverted configurations with the face-shaped noise is consistent with biases apparent in Figure 7A.
source: The preference for upright vs. inverted configurations with the face-shaped noise is consistent with biases apparent in Figure 7A.
evidence: This connects the inversion effect to the body orientation experiment, supported by Figure 7A.

claim: Face cells in ML were responsive to headless bodies at a variety of spatial positions, but activity tended to be strongest when bodies were positioned below the activating region.
source: Though face cells in ML were responsive to headless bodies at a variety of spatial positions, activity tended to be strongest when bodies were positioned below the activating region (Figure 7A; bottom two rows).
evidence: This describes the spatial specificity of the headless body response, supported by Figure 7A.

claim: For face-ambiguous stimulation, contextual responses are strongest to spatial configurations that reflect typical experience.
source: Thus, for face-ambiguous stimulation, contextual responses are strongest to spatial configurations that reflect typical experience.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the body orientation and inversion experiments.

claim: The development of face domains depends on seeing faces during development.
source: Alternatively, given that the development of face domains depends on seeing faces during development (Arcaro et al., 2017), these conjoint representations might also be learned over development as a consequence of frequently seeing faces and bodies together.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Arcaro et al., 2017).

claim: Conjoint representations of faces and bodies might be learned over development as a consequence of frequently seeing faces and bodies together.
source: Alternatively, given that the development of face domains depends on seeing faces during development (Arcaro et al., 2017), these conjoint representations might also be learned over development as a consequence of frequently seeing faces and bodies together.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: AlexNet was trained to classify natural images into 1000 object categories.
source: Specifically, we took a convolutional neural network, AlexNet (Krizevsky et al., 2012), trained to classify natural images into 1000 object categories, and assessed its activation patterns evoked by images of isolated objects from 6 different categories; human faces, headless human bodies, animals, houses, inanimate objects, and handheld tools (Figure 8A, top).
evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study, supported by Figure 8A.

claim: Images are distinguished along categorical distinctions even based on just pixel intensity.
source: As seen in the multidimensional scaling visualization, images are distinguished along categorical distinctions even based on just pixel intensity (Figure 8A, bottom).
evidence: This describes the representational structure at the pixel level, supported by Figure 8A.

claim: The Euclidean distances between image pairs within each category were smaller than between categories, indicating that images were more homogenous within than between categories.
source: The Euclidean distances between image pairs within each category were smaller than between categories, indicating that images were more homogenous within than between categories and highlighting that low-level features such as shape, color, or texture are a major component of these commonly tested 'semantic' categories (also see Dailey and Cottrell, 1999).
evidence: This describes the representational structure at the pixel level and is supported by citation to prior work (Dailey and Cottrell, 1999).

claim: Distinctions between categories were present in early layers of AlexNet.
source: Distinctions between categories were present in early layers of AlexNet (Figure 8A, bottom).
evidence: This describes the representational structure in early layers of AlexNet, supported by Figure 8A.

claim: The distinction between faces and non-faces persisted across all layers of AlexNet.
source: The distinction between faces and non-faces persisted across all layers of AlexNet.
evidence: This describes the representational structure across layers of AlexNet.

claim: The mean distance between face pairs was smaller than the mean distance between faces and non-body, non-face categories (animals, houses, objects, and tools).
source: The mean distance between face pairs (red) was smaller than the mean distance between faces and non-body, non-face categories (animals, houses, objects, and tools).
evidence: This describes the representational structure in AlexNet.

claim: Across all rectified linear unit (relu) layers of AlexNet, activation patterns were more similar for within category comparisons of both faces and bodies than between faces and other categories.
source: Across all rectified linear unit (relu) layers of AlexNet, activation patterns were more similar for within category comparisons of both faces and bodies (Figure 8B, solid red and green circles, Spearman rank correlations) than between faces and other categories (dual colored circles).
evidence: This describes the representational similarity in AlexNet, supported by Figure 8B.

claim: At the pixel level and in early layers of AlexNet, the mean similarity between faces and bodies was greater than the similarity between faces and the other categories.
source: At the pixel level and in early layers of AlexNet, the mean similarity between faces and bodies (half red/half green circles) was greater than the similarity between faces and the other categories; this similarity was also stronger to that obtained under randomization of the stimulus labels for non-face categories (this randomization distribution is marked by the grey shaded region that denotes 2.5% and 97.5% bounds).
evidence: This describes the representational similarity between faces and bodies in early layers of AlexNet.

claim: In the deeper layers of AlexNet (relu6 and relu7), face and body image representations become more overlapping.
source: In the deeper layers of AlexNet (relu6 and relu7), face and body image representations become more overlapping (Figure 8B, inset).
evidence: This describes the representational similarity between faces and bodies in deep layers of AlexNet, supported by Figure 8B.

claim: In relu7, the correlation between face and body image pairs were only slightly weaker than the correlation between pairs of body images.
source: In relu7, the correlation between face and body image pairs were only slightly weaker than the correlation between pairs of body images.
evidence: This describes the representational similarity between faces and bodies in relu7 of AlexNet.

claim: Untrained versions of AlexNet did not yield strong face-body correlations and these correlations were no different than correlations between faces and other categories.
source: Further, these results were specific to the trained AlexNet, as untrained versions of the network did not yield strong face-body correlations and these correlations were no different than correlations between faces and other categories (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This demonstrates that the face-body overlap in AlexNet is a result of training, supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Representations of faces and bodies can merge over learning without any explicit training about faces and bodies.
source: These results demonstrate that representations of faces and bodies can merge over learning without any explicit training about faces and bodies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AlexNet analysis.

claim: AlexNet was not trained to categorize faces, bodies, or even humans.
source: This is particularly impressive given that AlexNet was not trained to categorize faces, bodies, or even humans.
evidence: This is a fact about the AlexNet training procedure.

claim: Because faces and bodies co-occur in people and people were present in the training images, faces and bodies share variance in their informativeness with respect to class labels.
source: Because faces and bodies co-occur in people and people were present in the training images, faces and bodies share variance in their informativeness with respect to class labels.
evidence: This is an inference about why face and body representations merge in AlexNet.

claim: There is pressure for the network to use overlapping representations in the face and body hidden layer representations in this supervised learning scenario.
source: There is thus pressure for the network to use overlapping representations in the face and body hidden layer representations in this supervised learning scenario.
evidence: This is an inference about the learning dynamics in AlexNet.

claim: This phenomenon should hold more generally in unsupervised or self-supervised settings as the presence of image co-occurrence in the input would be expected to lead to similar overlap.
source: This phenomenon should hold more generally in unsupervised or self-supervised settings as the presence of image co-occurrence in the input would be expected to lead to similar overlap.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generality of the learning phenomenon.

claim: Convolutional networks can capture some aspects of the representational structure of biological networks.
source: Though convolutional networks can capture some aspects of the representational structure of biological networks (Hong et al., 2016; Ponce et al., 2019), these networks as currently implemented are not well suited for probing the retinotopic specificity of object representations, because they are explicitly constrained to process inputs from different portions of an image in the same way.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hong et al., 2016; Ponce et al., 2019).

claim: Convolutional networks as currently implemented are not well suited for probing the retinotopic specificity of object representations, because they are explicitly constrained to process inputs from different portions of an image in the same way.
source: Though convolutional networks can capture some aspects of the representational structure of biological networks (Hong et al., 2016; Ponce et al., 2019), these networks as currently implemented are not well suited for probing the retinotopic specificity of object representations, because they are explicitly constrained to process inputs from different portions of an image in the same way.
evidence: This is a limitation of convolutional networks for modeling retinotopic specificity.

claim: Previous neuronal recordings in macaques found that face-selective neurons respond only weakly to images of headless bodies, and body-selective neurons poorly to faces, suggesting that face and body circuits are largely independent.
source: Previous neuronal recordings in macaques found that face-selective neurons respond only weakly to images of headless bodies, and body-selective neurons poorly to faces, suggesting that face and body circuits are largely independent (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Freiwald et al., 2009; Kiani et al., 2007; Tsao et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neuronal recording studies (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Freiwald et al., 2009; Kiani et al., 2007; Tsao et al., 2006).

claim: Human fMRI studies have provided evidence that face and body processing are independent.
source: Human fMRI studies have also provided evidence that face and body processing are independent (Kaiser et al., 2014; Peelen and Downing, 2005; Peelen et al., 2006; Schwarzlose et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies (Kaiser et al., 2014; Peelen and Downing, 2005; Peelen et al., 2006; Schwarzlose et al., 2005).

claim: Face-selective domains in the FFA do not respond to headless animals or human bodies presented at fixation.
source: and that face-selective domains in the FFA do not respond to headless animals or human bodies presented at fixation (Kanwisher et al., 1999; Peelen and Downing, 2005; Schwarzlose et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies (Kanwisher et al., 1999; Peelen and Downing, 2005; Schwarzlose et al., 2005).

claim: The face neurons recorded from responded strongly and selectively to faces presented over a limited part of the visual field but did not respond to bodies presented to the same region.
source: Consistent with these prior findings, the face neurons we recorded from responded strongly and selectively to faces presented over a limited part of the visual field but did not respond to bodies presented to the same region.
evidence: This describes the basic response properties of the recorded neurons.

claim: These neurons also responded to masked and occluded faces that lacked intrinsic facial features, but were above bodies.
source: However, these neurons also responded to masked and occluded faces that lacked intrinsic facial features, but were above bodies.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study.

claim: When non-face objects that did not by themselves evoke a response from these neurons were placed above a body, the face-selective neurons fired robustly.
source: Further, when non-face objects that did not by themselves evoke a response from these neurons were placed above a body, the face-selective neurons fired robustly.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study.

claim: These neurons responded to bodies positioned such that the body implied the presence of a face within the neurons' activating regions.
source: Consistent across all six experiments, these neurons responded to bodies positioned such that the body implied the presence of a face within the neurons' activating regions.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study.

claim: Prior studies might have found larger responses to bodies if the bodies had been presented lower in the visual field, below the center of maximal activation to faces.
source: In prior studies, both headless bodies and faces were presented at fixation, so our results suggest that these studies might have found larger responses to bodies if the bodies had been presented lower in the visual field, below the center of maximal activation to faces.
evidence: This is a speculation about how prior studies might have obtained different results.

claim: The face fusiform area (FFA) in humans has been reported to be responsive to animal bodies with obscured faces.
source: The face fusiform area (FFA) in humans has been reported to be responsive to animal bodies with obscured faces (Chao et al., 1998) or to blurred faces above bodies (Cox et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies (Chao et al., 1998; Cox et al., 2004).

claim: Cox et al., 2004 found body-below facilitation of BOLD signal for blurred faces but not for clear faces.
source: Cox et al., 2004 also found body-below facilitation of BOLD signal for blurred faces but not for clear faces, and they found that the BOLD signal facilitation depended on the face and body being in a correct spatial configuration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior fMRI work (Cox et al., 2004).

claim: Cox et al., 2004 found that the BOLD signal facilitation depended on the face and body being in a correct spatial configuration.
source: Cox et al., 2004 also found body-below facilitation of BOLD signal for blurred faces but not for clear faces, and they found that the BOLD signal facilitation depended on the face and body being in a correct spatial configuration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior fMRI work (Cox et al., 2004).

claim: Both findings from Cox et al., 2004 are consistent with the neuronal recording results of this study.
source: Both these findings are consistent with our neuronal recording results.
evidence: This connects the current findings to prior fMRI work.

claim: The most anterior face patches show stronger fMRI activations to images of whole monkeys than to the sum of the responses to faces and to bodies.
source: In monkeys, the most anterior face patches show stronger fMRI activations to images of whole monkeys than to the sum of the responses to faces and to bodies; however, the middle and posterior face patches (which we recorded here) do not show facilitation, and have only sub-additive responses (Fisher and Freiwald, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior fMRI work (Fisher and Freiwald, 2015).

claim: The middle and posterior face patches do not show facilitation, and have only sub-additive responses.
source: In monkeys, the most anterior face patches show stronger fMRI activations to images of whole monkeys than to the sum of the responses to faces and to bodies; however, the middle and posterior face patches (which we recorded here) do not show facilitation, and have only sub-additive responses (Fisher and Freiwald, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior fMRI work (Fisher and Freiwald, 2015).

claim: fMRI studies are limited in that they can measure responses only of large populations of neurons of potentially mixed selectivity and therefore cannot resolve the relationship of face and body neural circuits.
source: Thus, although there is some fMRI evidence for interactions between face and body processing, fMRI studies are limited in that they can measure responses only of large populations of neurons of potentially mixed selectivity and therefore cannot resolve the relationship of face and body neural circuits.
evidence: This is a limitation of fMRI studies.

claim: By direct neuronal recording, face and body circuits are not independent and face-selective neurons can express large, complex, silent, contextual surround effects.
source: Here we show by direct neuronal recording that face and body circuits are not independent and that face-selective neurons can express large, complex, silent, contextual surround effects.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study.

claim: From simultaneously recording neurons in PL and ML face patches, contextual effects emerge fast and are first detected in the posterior patch, suggesting that contextual effects involve at least some feedforward inputs that cannot be attributed to cognitive processes such as mental imagery or expectation.
source: From simultaneously recording neurons in PL and ML face patches, we show that these responses emerge fast and are first detected in the posterior patch, suggesting that contextual effects involve at least some feedforward inputs that cannot be attributed to cognitive processes such as mental imagery or expectation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simultaneous recordings in PL and ML.

claim: If the feedforward inputs to face-selective neurons are sculpted by experience to be responsive not only to faces, but also to things frequently experienced in conjunction with faces, then such expectations would be manifest as the kind of complex response properties reported here.
source: However, if the feedforward inputs to, say, face-selective neurons, are sculpted by experience to be responsive not only to faces, but also to things frequently experienced in conjunction with faces, then such expectations would be manifest as the kind of complex response properties reported here.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism underlying the contextual effects.

claim: In contrast to the traditional view of a dichotomy of spatial and object vision, the data demonstrate that object processing in IT is spatially specific.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to the traditional view of a dichotomy of spatial and object vision, our data demonstrate that object processing in IT is spatially specific (also see Op De Beeck and Vogels, 2000).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings and is supported by citation to prior work (Op De Beeck and Vogels, 2000).

claim: Neurons in inferotemporal cortex do not code objects and complex shapes in isolation.
source: More broadly, these results highlight that neurons in inferotemporal cortex do not code objects and complex shapes in isolation.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study.

claim: These neurons are sensitive to the statistical regularities of their cumulative experience and the facilitation of face-selective neurons in the absence of a clear face reflects a lifetime of experience that bodies are usually accompanied by faces.
source: We propose that these neurons are sensitive to the statistical regularities of their cumulative experience and that the facilitation of face-selective neurons in the absence of a clear face reflects a lifetime of experience that bodies are usually accompanied by faces.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: An intrinsic retinotopic organization guides the subsequent development of category-selectivity in inferotemporal cortex, such as face and body domains.
source: Recently, we proposed that an intrinsic retinotopic organization (Arcaro and Livingstone, 2017; also see Hasson et al., 2002) guides the subsequent development of category-selectivity in inferotemporal cortex, such as face and body domains (Arcaro et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Arcaro and Livingstone, 2017; Hasson et al., 2002; Arcaro et al., 2017).

claim: Monkeys normally fixate faces, and they develop face domains within regions of inferotemporal cortex that represent central visual space.
source: For example, monkeys normally fixate faces, and they develop face domains within regions of inferotemporal cortex that represent central visual space (Figure 9, top).
evidence: This is an example of how retinotopic organization guides category selectivity, supported by Figure 9.

claim: The same developmental mechanisms can account for contextual learning.
source: Here, we propose that these same developmental mechanisms can account for contextual learning.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Just as the retinotopic regularity of experiencing faces guides where in IT face domains develop, the spatial regularity between faces and bodies is also learned in a retinotopic fashion and may account for why face and body patches stereotypically emerge in adjacent parts of cortex in both humans and monkeys.
source: Our results indicate that, just as the retinotopic regularity of experiencing faces guides where in IT face domains develop, the spatial regularity between faces and bodies is also learned in a retinotopic fashion and may account for why face and body patches stereotypically emerge in adjacent parts of cortex (Figure 9, bottom) in both humans (Schwarzlose et al., 2005) and monkeys (Bell et al., 2009; Pinsk et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, supported by Figure 9 and citations to prior work (Schwarzlose et al., 2005; Bell et al., 2009; Pinsk et al., 2009).

claim: Such a spatial regularity is consistent with prior observations of a lower visual field bias for the RF centers of body-selective neurons near ML and an upper visual field bias for eye-selective neurons in PL.
source: Such a spatial regularity is consistent with prior observations of a lower visual field bias for the RF centers of body-selective neurons near ML (Popivanov et al., 2015) and an upper visual field bias for eye-selective neurons in PL (Issa and DiCarlo, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Popivanov et al., 2015; Issa and DiCarlo, 2012).

claim: Something as complex and abstract as context may be firmly grounded in the ubiquitous mechanisms that govern the wiring-up of the brain across development.
source: Thus, something as complex and abstract as context may be firmly grounded in the ubiquitous mechanisms that govern the wiring-up of the brain across development (Arcaro et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings and is supported by citation to prior work (Arcaro et al., 2019).

claim: All procedures were approved in protocol (1146) by the Harvard Medical School Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), following the Guide for the care and use of laboratory animals (Ed 8).
source: All procedures were approved in protocol (1146) by the Harvard Medical School Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), following the Guide for the care and use of laboratory animals (Ed 8).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Two adult male macaques (10–12 kg) implanted with chronic microelectrode arrays were used in this experiment.
source: Two adult male macaques (10–12 kg) implanted with chronic microelectrode arrays were used in this experiment.
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: In monkey 1, two floating microelectrode arrays were implanted in the right hemisphere superior temporal sulcus – one within the posterior lateral (PL) face patch in posterior inferotemporal cortex (PIT) (32-channel Microprobes FMA) and a second array within the middle lateral (ML) face patch in central inferotemporal cortex (CIT) (128-channel NeuroNexus Matrix array).
source: In monkey 1, two floating microelectrode arrays were implanted in the right hemisphere superior temporal sulcus – one within the posterior lateral (PL) face patch in posterior inferotemporal cortex (PIT) (32-channel Microprobes FMA; https://microprobes.com/products/multichannel-arrays/fma) and a second array within the middle lateral (ML) face patch in central inferotemporal cortex (CIT) (128-channel NeuroNexus Matrix array; http://neuronexus.com/products/primate-large-brain/matrix-array-primate/).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup for monkey 1.

claim: In monkey 2, one 32-channel floating microelectrode array was implanted in left hemisphere ML.
source: In monkey 2, one 32-channel floating microelectrode array was implanted in left hemisphere ML.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup for monkey 2.

claim: Monkeys were trained to perform a fixation task.
source: Monkeys were trained to perform a fixation task.
evidence: This describes the behavioral task used in the study.

claim: Neural recordings were performed on a 64-channel Plexon Omniplex Acquisition System.
source: Neural recordings were performed on a 64-channel Plexon Omniplex Acquisition System.
evidence: This describes the recording system used in the study.

claim: For monkey 1, recordings were performed simultaneously for the 32-ch PIT array and 32-ch from the CIT array.
source: For monkey 1, recordings were performed simultaneously for the 32-ch PIT array and 32-ch from the CIT array.
evidence: This describes the recording procedure for monkey 1.

claim: In both monkeys, the same channels were recorded from for each experimental session.
source: In both monkeys, the same channels were recorded from for each experimental session.
evidence: This describes the recording procedure.

claim: The task required the monkey to keep their gaze within ± 0.75° of a 0.25° fixation spot.
source: The task required the monkey to keep their gaze within ± 0.75° of a 0.25° fixation spot.
evidence: This describes the fixation task.

claim: An ISCAN eye monitoring system was used to track eye movements.
source: We used an ISCAN eye monitoring system to track eye movements (www.iscaninccom).
evidence: This describes the eye tracking system used in the study.
